item.title: Aargau Cantonal Taxes: Rates and Deductions
item.description: Find out how cantonal and municipal taxes work in the Canton of Aargau, including progressive tax rates, allowable deductions, and how to file your taxes online. A practical guide.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Swiss cantonal taxes are divided into three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal - In the Canton of Aargau, each municipality has its own multiplier for cantonal tax - Allowable deductions vary by canton and municipality - The Aargau online portal allows for digital tax filings
## Key Facts - **What**: Three-tier tax structure (federal + cantonal + municipal) - Where: Canton of Aargau, northeastern Switzerland - Who: Aargau Cantonal Tax Administration, local municipalities - Deadlines: Annual tax return (dates vary by canton) - Deductions: Professional expenses, mortgage interest, insurance premiums, AVS/LPP contributions
In Switzerland, the tax system is organized into three distinct levels: direct federal tax (IFD), cantonal taxes, and municipal taxes. The Canton of Aargau, located in northeastern Switzerland, follows this national framework, with each municipality responsible for collecting municipal tax by applying a multiplier to the cantonal tax rate.
In the Canton of Aargau, as in all Swiss cantons, the cantonal tax system allows for specific deductions from taxable income: professional expenses, mortgage interest, health insurance premiums, and contributions to pension plans (AVS, LPP, third pillar 3a). The progressive tax bracket structure ensures that the tax increases gradually with income, without sudden jumps.
### How the Municipal Multiplier Works
Each municipality applies its own multiplier to the cantonal tax rate, allowing for local flexibility in tax collection. A multiplier of 100 means the municipality collects 100% of the cantonal tax rate; values greater than 100 indicate an additional municipal tax. This structure allows Aargau municipalities to finance local services while maintaining a uniform tax base with the canton.
The Aargau Cantonal Tax Administration provides an online portal where taxpayers can file their returns digitally, view information on allowable deductions, and access official forms. Filing deadlines vary annually; for current details, the official website of the cantonal administration is the primary source.
### Tax Rates and Brackets
The Canton of Aargau applies progressive tax rates based on fixed income brackets set by the canton. The standard tax rates and specific brackets can be viewed directly on the cantonal tax administration’s portal, which ensures that the information is always up to date. [Dichiarazione online](nav:tax-return). These may undergo minor changes each year due to inflation adjustments or cantonal policy decisions, so it is essential to verify the relevant tax year. ### Allowable Deductions and Their Impact
The deductions allowed in the Canton of Aargau reduce taxable income and, consequently, the total amount of tax due. Among the main deductions are professional expenses (costs directly related to work, supplies, work-related transportation, and professional training), mortgage interest (generally deductible on real estate loans), insurance premiums (especially health and supplemental insurance), and social security contributions (payments to AVS/AHV, LPP/BVG, and the third pillar 3a with an annual limit).
The value of a deduction depends on the marginal tax rate: a higher-income worker benefits more from a CHF 100 deduction than a lower-income worker, because each franc saved falls into a higher tax bracket.
### Practical Scenarios: Before-and-After Comparison of Deductions
Scenario A: An employee in the Canton of Aargau with a gross annual income of CHF 65,000 deducts CHF 5,000 in mortgage interest and CHF 3,000 in LPP contributions (7% of the coordinated salary, example for the 25–34 age group). Taxable income: CHF 57,000. If the average cantonal tax rate (including the municipal multiplier) were approximately X%, the tax calculated on CHF 57,000 would be lower than that on CHF 65,000.
Scenario B: The same employee without itemized deductions pays the full tax on CHF 65,000, without any tax reduction benefits. The difference between the two scenarios is why it is crucial to track all deductible expenses and report them correctly on the tax return.
### The Role of the Paycheck and Withholding Tax
Throughout the year, the employer withholds provisional tax from the paycheck based on simplified federal and cantonal tax brackets. This withholding is not the final tax; it serves as an advance payment. When filing the annual tax return, actual deductions, final tax brackets, and the final balance are calculated. If the withholding exceeded the actual tax owed, the taxpayer receives a refund; if it was less, the taxpayer must pay the difference. [busta paga svizzera](nav:payslip).
This mechanism makes the annual tax return in the Canton of Aargau an essential step for every resident, whether an employee or self-employed.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Tax Filing Procedure in the Canton of Aargau
To file your cantonal taxes in the Canton of Aargau, follow these steps:
**Step 1: Gather Your Documents** Gather your wage statements (pay stubs for the year, bank statements for other income), deduction documents (mortgage interest invoices, LPP/third-pillar account statements, insurance receipts, and business expense documents).
Step 2: Access the online portal Visit the official website of the Aargau Cantonal Tax Administration. The platform provides access to the interactive tax return form and documentation on allowable deductions for the current tax year. Registration requires a taxpayer ID number (provided in previous tax documents) and online access.
Step 3: Filling out the tax return Enter your total income, allowable deductions by category, and pension contributions paid. The portal automatically calculates your taxable income based on the canton’s progressive tax brackets and the municipal multiplier specific to your municipality of residence.
Step 4: Review and Submission Review the summary and verify the automatic calculations (applied tax rates, tax brackets). Submit your return digitally by the annual deadline. The system will provide a confirmation receipt.
Step 5: Receiving the Tax Assessment The cantonal tax administration will issue the tax assessment notice within a few months of the deadline. If refunds are due, they will be credited to your bank account within the specified timeframe. If an additional payment is due, you will receive payment instructions.
### Annual Deadlines and Useful Contacts
The filing deadlines for the Aargau cantonal tax return are set annually by the tax administration. They generally fall in the spring (March–May), but it is essential to check the official calendar on the portal for the relevant tax year: no automatic extension is guaranteed without a formal request to the canton.
Contacts: Aargau Online Tax Return Portal — access via the Cantonal Tax Administration’s website; Phone Help Desk — available during business hours (hours listed on the website); Email for specific inquiries — addresses available on the portal.
Use [calcolatore delle imposte](nav:calculator) to estimate your tax liability and prepare a projection before filing your return. This tool helps you see how deductions and tax rates affect your total tax liability.

item.title: Wages and the Labor Market in Graubünden
item.description: Sectors with job openings, salary levels by education level, and collective bargaining agreements in the Canton of Graubünden: a guide to the Swiss system.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Wages in Graubünden follow federal regulations; there is no cantonal minimum wage - Mandatory deductions: AVS/AI 5.3%, LPP 7–18% depending on age, private LAMal 300–2,500 CHF - Maximum 45 hours/week (office work), minimum 4 days of vacation, 2 weeks of paternity leave - Check salaries using the SECO calculator and FSO/BFS for sector-specific data
## Key Facts - **What**: Wage structure and salary determination in the Canton of Graubünden - When: Systems in effect in 2026 - Where: Canton of Graubünden, in accordance with Swiss federal laws - Who: Employees, employers, SECO, cantonal employment office - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% employee, 10.6% total (including employer) - LPP contributions: 7% (ages 25–34), 10% (ages 35–44), 15% (ages 45–54), 18% (55+) - LAMal: Mandatory, deductibles 300–2,500 CHF, premiums vary by canton - Weekly hours: Max 45 hours (office/sales), 50 hours (other sectors)
The Canton of Graubünden follows the same Swiss federal principles for determining wages. Unlike some cantons (Geneva, Ticino, Basel-Stadt, Vaud, Jura, Neuchâtel), Graubünden has not established its own cantonal minimum wage. The standard remains the sector-specific collective bargaining agreement (CBA)—where applicable—or individual negotiation between the employee and employer. This does not mean a lack of protection: CBAs registered at the federal level guarantee sector-specific minimum wages for office work, retail, construction, healthcare, and the hospitality industry.
The economic sectors that hire workers in the Canton of Graubünden include tourism and hospitality, services, agriculture, construction, small-scale manufacturing, healthcare, and public administration. All companies must comply with federal requirements: a maximum workweek of 45 hours for office work, retail, and industry (50 hours for other sectors), a minimum of 4 weeks of annual vacation, and a prohibition on wage discrimination based on gender.
### Education and Wage Levels
The wage structure in the Canton of Graubünden reflects standard Swiss criteria: educational attainment is the primary factor driving wage differences. An employee with a Federal Certificate of Competence (AFC) earns a lower salary than someone with an advanced vocational qualification, and even less than someone who has completed tertiary education (university, higher vocational school, master’s degree). This hierarchy varies by sector: in the office sector, the difference can reach 35–40%; in construction, 20–25%; and in services, 20–30%.
Work experience and seniority lead to progressive pay increases: collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) often establish seniority scales. The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) publishes annual median wages by canton, sector, and education level, providing a benchmark for the Graubünden labor market. An employee negotiating a salary can check whether the offer received is in line with the national and cantonal medians. ### Mandatory Contributions and Social Protection
Every paycheck in Switzerland, and therefore in the Canton of Grisons, includes mandatory deductions to fund [social security](nav:pension). The **old-age and survivors' insurance (AHV)** and disability insurance (IV) require a contribution of 5.3% from the employee; the employer contributes an additional 5.3% (total 10.6%). Unemployment insurance (ALV) and employer insolvency compensation (EIB) absorb 0.55% from the employee up to an annual maximum. Accident insurance (UVG) is paid only by the employer (0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector).
The second pillar, occupational pension (BVG/LPP), represents the company pension fund. It is mandatory for coordinated salaries — typically starting from around 22'000 CHF annually (the coordination threshold varies each year). The BVG/LPP contribution is progressive by age bracket: 7% for those aged 25 to 34, 10% for those aged 35 to 44, 15% for those aged 45 to 54, and 18% from age 55 until the reference age (65 for men, 64 for women). In the Canton of Grisons, it is the employer who negotiates the terms of the BVG/LPP plan with an insurance company and communicates the details to the employees.
### LAMal and Health Insurance
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for every resident in Switzerland but represents a private policy, not a salary deduction. The worker must take it out within 3 months of settling in Switzerland. Premiums vary by canton and geographical region, as well as by age bracket and LAMal [deductible model](nav:health). In the Canton of Grisons, there are various tariff regions and multiple competing health insurance funds. Available deductibles range from 300 CHF to 2'500 CHF annually; a lower deductible results in higher monthly premiums, and vice versa. The Canton provides subsidies to low-income households to cover part of the premium.
A common mistake is forgetting that LAMal does not appear on the paycheck: the premium is paid directly by the employee to the health insurance fund. To verify if the premiums are competitive, the worker can consult the comparison tool promoted by the Canton or contact a health insurance fund operating in Grisons.
### Collective Labor Agreements and Minimum Wage
In the Canton of Grisons, sectors such as hospitality, construction, trade, healthcare, and public services are often covered by collective labor agreements (CLA) registered at the federal level. A CLA specifies: minimum wages by category (waiter, bricklayer, salesperson), probation period, seniority increases, night, Sunday, or holiday work allowances, union rights, internal complaint procedure. Those working in a company covered by a CLA are automatically protected by these minimum standards.
Those working in companies not covered by a CLA depend on individual agreements. Grisons has not set a cantonal minimum wage, so in the absence of a CLA, the reference remains direct negotiation. If a worker suspects they are being paid below the CLA applicable to their sector, they can check the full text on the SECO portal, contact the relevant union, or turn to the cantonal control authority.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure for Checking and Reading Your Pay stub
To verify whether a paycheck is correct, the employee must first read and understand their [busta paga svizzera](nav:payslip). The main components are: **gross salary** (contractual amount before deductions), AVS/AI deductions (5.3%), AD/AC deductions (up to 0.55% up to the annual cap), LPP contribution (if applicable, ranging from 7% to 18% depending on age), advance income tax withholding (cantonal and municipal, proportional to gross pay and the canton of residence), and finally net pay (the amount actually deposited into the account). LAMal does not appear on the pay stub because it is a separately purchased policy.
An [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) tool allows you to quickly estimate your monthly take-home pay based on your gross pay by selecting the canton (Grisons), industry, age, and tax bracket. This tool helps you evaluate a job offer before accepting it or verify that your current paycheck is correct. The Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) publishes annual median wages by canton, sector, and education level—an essential reference for comparing your salary to the market.
### When Your Salary Is Incorrect: Appeals and Procedures
If an employee discovers an error or an unjustified omission in their salary—for example, a deduction that was never agreed upon, a failure to adjust pay in accordance with the collective bargaining agreement (CBA), or an unlawful deduction—they must take action in stages. First step: Submit a written request to the employer, specifying the disputed item and citing the relevant provision in the individual employment contract or the collective bargaining agreement (CBA). Second step: Review the full text of the applicable CBA (available on the SECO website) or consult a guide from the relevant trade union to verify whether a violation has occurred.
If the dispute persists, the employee can contact the relevant cantonal authority—in the Canton of Graubünden, the cantonal employment office—or seek assistance from a sector-specific union (which sometimes offers free advice to members). Contractual notice periods are standardized at the federal level: the employer may terminate the contract with one month’s notice during the first year of employment, two months’ notice from the second to the ninth year, and three months’ notice from the tenth year onward. If an employee believes they have been unlawfully terminated or dismissed in response to a complaint (retaliation), they may file a claim with the competent cantonal civil courts, possibly with the assistance of an attorney specializing in labor law.

item.title: Daycare and Childcare in Basel-Landschaft: Costs
item.description: Fees and Subsidies for Daycare and Childcare in Basel-Landschaft. How income-based fees work and what financial assistance is available.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Cantonal childcare services: daycare centers, family daycare providers, after-school programs - Income-based fees with subsidies available - Easy access: contact your municipality’s Social Services Office - Costs range from CHF 200–700 per month, depending on income
## Key Facts - **What**: Child care services (daycare centers, family daycare providers, after-school programs) - Where: Canton of Basel-Landschaft, northwestern Switzerland - Who: Cantonal administration and municipalities - Jurisdiction: Cantonal—each canton has its own regulations - Fees: Calculated based on family income, with subsidies available
Child care in Switzerland is organized under a cantonal jurisdiction model. In the Canton of Basel-Landschaft, as in all Swiss cantons, the cantonal administration and municipalities manage child care services, ensuring access to various types of facilities with fees calculated based on family income.
### Why Responsibility Lies with the Cantons
Unlike other European countries where childcare is regulated at the national level, in Switzerland each canton has complete autonomy over regulations, quality standards, fee structures, and available subsidies. This means that the childcare system in Basel-Landschaft has its own unique characteristics, even though it follows principles common throughout Switzerland: professional quality, fair fees based on income, and equal access for all families.
### Types of Facilities Available
Daycare centers (Kindertagesstätten) care for children from a few weeks old up to 4–5 years old, offering full-time or part-time care depending on family needs. Daycare families (Tagesfamilien) are run by accredited caregivers who care for small groups in their own homes, often with more flexible hours. After-school programs (Hort) support school-age children after school with recreational activities and homework help.
### Income-Based Fee System
In Basel-Landschaft, as in many Swiss cantons, fees are calculated based on the family’s net income. A cantonal formula determines the percentage of the hourly fee paid by each family: those with lower incomes pay less, while those with higher incomes pay more, up to a maximum percentage (usually between 80% and 100%). Cantonal subsidies further reduce the burden on families in financial difficulty; these are often automatically deducted from the bill. ### Cantonal Costs and Subsidies
In the canton of Basel-Landschaft, the cost structure for child care combines three main elements: the basic hourly rate, the income-based calculation, and any cantonal subsidy.
The base hourly rate varies depending on the type of facility (daycare center vs. family daycare) and the location within the canton. However, this standard rate is not applied uniformly to all families: each family pays a percentage of the total cost based on its net income. Families with lower incomes may pay 10–30% of the standard rate, while those with higher incomes pay a higher percentage, up to 100%. This progressive structure ensures that the cost of childcare remains affordable regardless of a family’s financial situation.
### Cantonal Subsidies and Additional Assistance
Cantonal subsidies form the second pillar of the system. The canton of Basel-Landschaft provides public funds to further reduce fees for families facing financial hardship. These subsidies are often automatically applied when calculating the final fee, without requiring separate applications from the family. Some municipalities in Basel-Landschaft also offer additional reductions for the second and third child, or increased subsidies for single-parent families.
### Example Scenarios
To understand how this works in practice: a single-income family with two children and an annual income of CHF 45,000 might pay CHF 300–400 per month for full-time daycare, after the income-based fee structure and cantonal subsidy have been applied. A family with an income of CHF 80,000 might pay CHF 600–700 per month for the same service. A family with an income exceeding CHF 120,000 might pay close to the full rate (approximately CHF 800–1,000 per month). These figures are approximate and vary significantly depending on the specific regulations of the municipality of residence within Basel-Landschaft and the city council’s annual decisions regarding subsidies.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to Access Services
Access to child care services in Basel-Landschaft follows a standardized procedure at the cantonal level, although there may be variations depending on your municipality of residence.
Step 1: Get information from your municipality Contact the Social Services Office (Sozialamt) in your municipality of residence. There, you will receive information on: a list of public and private childcare facilities available in the area (daycare centers, family daycare providers, after-school programs), enrollment procedures, the fee calculation model specific to your municipality, and details on available subsidies based on your financial situation.
**Step 2: Required Documentation** To qualify for income-based fees and financial assistance, you’ll need: a copy of the previous year’s tax return, a certificate of residence issued by the municipality, personal information for all family members, and (if applicable for separated families) a custody agreement signed with the other parent.
Step 3: Enrollment in the Childcare Facility Once you’ve identified an available facility, you’ll submit an enrollment application. The facility will coordinate with the Social Services Office to calculate your personalized fee based on your documents. Waiting times range from a few months to 1–2 years, especially for full-time daycare centers during periods of high demand. It is advisable to enroll at least 6–12 months in advance to increase your chances of securing a spot.
Step 4: Paying Fees The personalized fee will be billed monthly directly by the facility or the municipality. The cantonal subsidy will be automatically deducted from the bill according to the established procedures. Many facilities and municipalities also accept installment payments or payment extensions for special financial circumstances.
### Realistic Timeline and What to Expect
It may take 2–6 weeks from registration to the first month of attendance for tax documents to be processed and the personalized fee to be calculated. During this period, the Social Services Office will review your tax return and determine the amount of the subsidy to which you are entitled. Once approved, you will receive an official notification with the final monthly rate and the start date of childcare.
### Contacts and Resources
For detailed information specific to your municipality of residence, you can contact: the official portal of the Canton of Basel-Landschaft (basellandschaft.ch), your municipality’s Social Services Office, and the cantonal organizations that manage public and state-recognized childcare facilities. Keep in mind that cantonal regulations are updated annually, particularly regarding subsidy rates and base rates. It’s always best to check directly with the cantonal authorities to get the most up-to-date information.
Use the [calcolatore costi della custodia](nav:calculator) tool to estimate how much childcare might cost you based on your household income and the number of children.

item.title: Apprenticeships in Switzerland: How to Get Started
item.description: Dual system, contracts, pay, and vocational certification: everything you need to know about apprenticeships in the canton of Basel-Landschaft and throughout Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance
- Dual apprenticeship: 3–4 years split between vocational school and a company - AFC (Certificate of Competence): nationally recognized certificate - No federal minimum wage: compensation agreed upon between the company and the apprentice - Guaranteed rights: minimum vacation time, legal protection, AVS/AI/IPG social security contributions
## Key Facts
- **What**: Vocational training through the Swiss dual system - Where: Cantonal jurisdiction (including the canton of Basel-Landschaft) - Duration: Typically 3–4 years - Certificate: AFC (Federal Certificate of Competence) - Federal agency: SECO coordinates the national vocational training system
An apprenticeship in Switzerland is not a traditional school-based education. It is a dual-track program that combines on-the-job training at a company (3–4 days per week) with vocational school (1 day per week), and is recognized at the federal level through the Federal Certificate of Professional Competence (AFC). In the canton of Basel-Landschaft, as in other Swiss cantons, there is an office dedicated to vocational training that oversees programs, contracts, and final exams.
### How the Dual System Works
The model is simple: the apprentice signs a contract with a company and attends vocational school at the same time. The company teaches the practical aspects of the trade, while the school provides general and vocational theory. At the end of the 3–4 years, the apprentice takes the final exam to earn the AFC, a qualification recognized throughout Switzerland.
In addition to the AFC, it is possible to earn the vocational matura, a complementary diploma that grants direct admission to universities of applied sciences (SUP) without additional exams. The vocational matura is earned during the apprenticeship or immediately afterward, depending on the canton and the chosen program. ### Where to Look for an Apprenticeship
The search for an apprenticeship usually begins 12–24 months before the planned start date. The main channels are national online portals, websites of companies in the sector of interest, the cantonal vocational training office, career fairs and open houses at companies, and school guidance counselors. In the canton of Basel-Landschaft, the cantonal vocational training office can provide lists of companies hiring apprentices, information on available programs, and application procedures.
Consult the cantonal vocational training office to identify opportunities available in your field. The application must be submitted directly to the chosen company, along with a resume, a cover letter, and academic transcripts.
### The Apprenticeship Contract: What It Contains
Once accepted by the company, the apprentice signs an **apprenticeship contract** (apprenticeship agreement). This document must include the apprentice’s and company’s details, the start and end dates of the apprenticeship, the occupation and training program (AFC), weekly working hours (maximum 45–50 hours depending on the sector), monthly compensation (agreed-upon amount), annual leave (at least 4–5 weeks depending on age), conditions for terminating the contract (probationary period, notice of termination), and references to the vocational school and its curriculum.
The contract must comply with the Federal Act on Vocational Education and Training (LFPr) and cantonal regulations. Before signing, it is advisable to read it carefully or have it reviewed by an advisor.
### Rights and Responsibilities of the Apprentice
The apprentice has rights guaranteed by federal law. The maximum workweek is 45 hours in most sectors (manufacturing, office work, retail) or 50 hours in other sectors (agriculture, skilled trades). The minimum annual vacation is 4 weeks (5 weeks for those under 20). The employer cannot terminate the contract arbitrarily: during the first month (probationary period), the contract may be terminated without notice; thereafter, a notice period (usually 2 weeks) must be observed.
Health and safety protections are mandatory: the employer must provide a safe work environment and comply with safety regulations (LAINF, workers’ compensation insurance). The employer pays mandatory social security contributions (AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC) and enrolls employees in occupational pension funds (LPP). If the apprentice is pregnant or a father, they are entitled to paid leave (14 weeks at 80% for maternity; 2 weeks for paternity). The apprentice has certain duties: to attend vocational school regularly, to follow the company’s instructions, to maintain confidentiality regarding company information, and to comply with safety regulations.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Apprentice Compensation
There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland, either for regular employees or for apprentices. Compensation is agreed upon between the apprentice and the company, within a market range that varies by sector, canton, and vocational field. However, some cantons (including Basel-Landschaft) have set cantonal minimum wages for apprentices in certain sectors. It is advisable to consult your cantonal vocational training office to find out the applicable thresholds in your canton.
In general, apprentices’ wages increase over the course of their training: the first year has the lowest wage, while the second and third years see increases of 10–20%, as does the fourth year (if applicable). In addition to wages, the company pays mandatory social security contributions: AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% of gross wages, split between the employee and the company), unemployment insurance (AD), and insolvency benefits (AC) up to an annual cap, accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) depending on the sector (0.7–1.5%), and a professional pension fund (LPP) if applicable.
The apprentice receives a net salary, meaning it is net of the social security contributions (AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC) already paid by the employer. Direct federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes are withheld or paid via an annual tax return. The gross and net amounts must be clearly indicated on the pay stub.
### Step-by-step: How to Apply
1. Research and Select a Company — Identify sectors and companies of interest at least 12–24 months before the planned start date. Visit company websites, check national job portals, and speak with career counselors.
2. Preparing your application — Write a resume (brief, 1 page) including personal information, education, and work experience. Write a cover letter (half a page) explaining why you’ve chosen that profession and that company. Request a letter of recommendation or attach your most recent academic transcripts.
3. Submitting Your Application — Send your application to the company (by mail, email, or in person). Be sure to include your resume, cover letter, and any attachments as specified by the company.
4. Job Interview — If you’re a good fit, the company will invite you for an interview. Prepare examples to demonstrate your motivation, ask thoughtful questions about the program, dress appropriately, arrive on time, and be polite.
5. Signing the Contract — If accepted, you’ll receive the apprenticeship contract. Read it carefully, ask questions, and keep a copy.
6. Enrollment in Vocational School — The company will enroll you in the appropriate vocational school. You’ll receive the class schedule and course materials.
If you’re interested in learning more about vocational training opportunities in the canton of Basel-Landschaft, visit the cantonal vocational training office to view available companies and contract terms. Use [calcolatore di stipendio](nav:calculator) to estimate your monthly take-home pay based on a hypothetical gross salary, taking into account AVS/AI/IPG social security contributions, AD/AC unemployment insurance, and federal income tax. This will help you plan your personal budget during your apprenticeship.

item.title: Apprenticeship in the canton of Basel-Country
item.description: How to find an internship in the canton of Basel-Country, the training contract, salary, social contributions and the path to professional maturity.

## In brief - Swiss professional training combines company internship and school teaching for 3-4 years - Mandatory written internship contract with salary, duration, and job description - Apprentices pay AVS/AI/IPG contributions from the first day of work
## Key facts - **What**: Dual training (company + school) leading to a federal certificate (EFA) or professional maturity - When: 3-4 year internship; typical start after compulsory schooling - Where: Canton of Basel-Landschaft, according to Swiss federal regulation - Who: Company, vocational school, cantonal education office, professional orientation center - Requirement: Written contract with employer before start
### How professional training works in Basel-Landschaft In the Swiss system, professional training is the most common path after compulsory schooling. The canton of Basel-Landschaft, like all cantons, follows the federal dual training model: the apprentice works in the company (3-4 days a week) and attends vocational school (1-2 days a week). The internship contract is the fundamental document. It must contain: - Start date and total duration - Description of professional activity - Gross monthly salary (variable by sector and canton) - Working hours (maximum 45 hours per week for industry and offices) - Duration of the trial period (typically 3 months) - Right to holidays (minimum 4 weeks annually; 5 for those under 20) - Provisions on illness, accident, special leaves The apprentice's remuneration is not subject to a federal minimum wage, but many cantons set their own minimums. In the canton of Basel-Landschaft, salaries vary by sector (crafts, trade, industry, services) and increase progressively over the years of the internship. The apprentice is subject to federal pension obligations: from the first day of work, they pay AVS/AI/IPG contributions (5.3% of gross salary; the employer contributes 10.6%). If the salary exceeds CHF 3,725 annually (2026), AD/AC contributions (1.1%) are added. Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory and independent of remuneration. Many apprentices also contribute to professional pension schemes (LPP/BVG), with percentages determined by age class. ### Contract and remuneration: what to know
The traineeship contract is a binding agreement between the trainee and the company, often mediated by the Training Office of the canton Basel-Country or by the Vocational Guidance Centre. A copy must be given to the apprentice before commencement; no modification is valid without written agreement.
Compensation is not uniform: it depends on the sector and the canton Basel-Country may apply sector-specific guidelines (even if Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage). Typically: - First year: lower amount (training phase fee) - Subsequent years: progressive increase, sometimes with predefined steps in the contract
An internship in the technical sector could start from CHF 500-600 per month in the 1st year and grow to CHF 900-1'100 in the 4th year (indicative figures that vary by company and sector). You can check the net to take home using our [calcolatore di busta paga](nav:payslip).
### Social contributions and coverage
Once the contract is signed, the apprentice is automatically enrolled in the following systems:
**AVS/AI/IPG**: The apprentice pays 5.3% of the gross salary. The employer pays 10.6% (both to the federal fund through the central deposit).
Unemployment Insurance (AD) and Insolvency Insurance (AC): If the annual salary exceeds CHF 3,725 (2026 annual ceiling), the AD/AC contribution of 1.1% is triggered up to the limit of CHF 148'200 of insured salary.
