## In a nutshell - Ordinary naturalization: permit C + 10 years federal residence - Basel City applies specific cantonal and municipal requirements - German language test (Swiss standard) usually required - Taxes and procedures vary between municipalities
## Key facts - **What**: Ordinary naturalization with C permit for at least 10 years - Where: Canton Basel City (municipalities: Basel, Riehen, Bettingen, others) - Who: Foreigners with a C permit established for at least 10 years - Requirements: Socio-cultural integration, knowledge of German language - Procedure: Question to the municipality, cantonal assessment - Taxes: Amounts defined by each municipality
### The federal framework of ordinary naturalization
Ordinary naturalization in Switzerland is based on stable federal criteria: those who wish to acquire Swiss citizenship must have had a C (domicile) permit for at least ten years. In the Canton of Basel-City, the competent municipalities (Basel, Riehen, Bettingen and others) add their own requirements in addition to federal legislation.
The procedure begins with an application submitted to the municipality of residence, which then forwards the application to the cantonal authorities for final assessment. Integration and German language tests constitute ordinary components in the assessment, although the details and modalities vary according to the municipality concerned.
### Who can access ordinary naturalization
Swiss federal law states that a foreign person may access ## Cantonal and Municipal Procedures in Basel-Stadt In the Canton of Basel-Stadt, the naturalization procedure is not uniform for all municipalities. Each municipality (Basel, Riehen, Bettingen, Birsfelden, and others) defines specific modalities and timelines, although the reference framework remains federal. The application must be submitted with a series of standard documents: extract from the residents' register, certificate of good conduct, evidence of integration (work, volunteering, civic participation), proof of language knowledge. Some municipalities may require additional certificates related to economic, family, or housing situations. Once the application is submitted to the municipality, it undergoes a publication phase (opposition period) during which citizens and authorities can raise objections. If there are no significant objections, the file is passed to the cantonal authorities for final approval. ### Naturalization Fees and Amounts The fees for naturalization vary significantly between Swiss municipalities and even within the same canton. In the Canton of Basel-Stadt, each municipality applies its own amounts, which generally range from a few hundred to a few thousand Swiss francs. It is essential to verify the current amounts directly with the municipality of residence, as these can change annually. Some municipalities offer the possibility to pay the fees in installments, but this option varies from municipality to municipality. Contact your municipal office to learn about the available payment methods. ### Procedure Timeline The overall timeline from the submission of the application to the final approval depends on multiple factors: completeness of the documentation, results of language and integration tests, number of files being processed by the municipality and the canton, any objections during the publication phase. On average, the process takes months (not days), but the Canton of Basel-Stadt has not publicly communicated standardized fixed deadlines. It is prudent to expect variable times depending on the municipality and the season (some periods present higher workloads). ### Fiscal Implications and Post-Naturalization Benefits Once naturalized, you will have access to the same fiscal benefits and duties as Swiss citizens. This includes the annual obligation to submit the federal and cantonal direct tax return through the [tax return procedure](nav:tax-return), the right to participate in federal, cantonal, and municipal votes, and full social and pension rights (including AHV and LPP). ### Appeals and Recourses in Case of Denial If a naturalization application is rejected, it is possible to appeal to the competent cantonal authorities within specific deadlines (usually 30 days from the denial). The appeal must detail the reasons why you believe the decision is incorrect or unfair. The cantonal authorities will review your file according to the formal procedure provided.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Step-by-step operational procedure
Step 1: Verify federal prerequisites. Ensure you have held a C permit (residence) for at least ten years. If your residence in Switzerland is less than this limit, you will have to wait. Certain periods (e.g., 8-18 years) count double according to federal regulations, thus reducing the overall time.
Step 2: Contact your municipality. Identify the competent office in the municipality where you reside (civil registry office, naturalization administrative office, or similar). Basel-Stadt includes Basel, Riehen, Bettingen, Birsfelden, Bottmingen, Münchenstein, and other municipalities: each has a specific point of contact. Request the required documentation and submission methods.
Step 3: Gather the necessary documents. Prepare a recent extract from the residents' register (generally not older than 3 months), a certificate of good conduct, proof of work and civic integration, and certificates of knowledge of Swiss German. The municipality may request additional documents based on your situation.
**Step 4: Submit the application.** Submit the complete application to the municipality, preferably in person or according to the communicated methods. Ensure you include all required documentation and receive a submission receipt.
Step 5: Wait for the publication phase. The municipality will publish your application for a set period (generally 30-60 days). During this period, anyone can raise justified objections regarding your eligibility or integration issues.
Step 6: Pass the tests (if required). If the municipality requires it, you must take the Swiss German language test and the integration test according to the methods and dates communicated by the office.
Step 7: Cantonal approval and issuance of the certificate. If everything proceeds positively and there are no objections, the file is forwarded to the cantonal authorities for final approval. Once approved, you will receive the Swiss citizenship certificate.
## Practical tools and resources
For detailed information specific to your municipality in Basel-Stadt, contact the competent municipal offices directly. The canton and municipalities provide online guides and telephone support. Federal resources (SEM - State Secretariat for Migration) offer overviews of the standard federal procedure.
[Use our tax calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the tax impact of naturalization on your income situation in Switzerland and understand how your contribution obligations will change.
If you currently work as a cross-border commuter and reside in another country, consult our in-depth analysis on [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to evaluate your post-naturalization economic budget.
If you are looking for [new job opportunities](nav:jobs) after naturalization, you will be able to access the Swiss job market without restrictions due to residence permits.
## Practical checklist for naturalization
- ☐ Verify your status: C permit for 10 years? (Periods 8-18 years count double) - ☐ Contact your municipality of residence - ☐ Request the official list of required documents - ☐ Prepare extract from the register and certificates of good conduct - ☐ Gather proof of socio-cultural and work integration - ☐ Schedule the language test if required by the municipality - ☐ Submit the complete application and keep the receipt

item.title: Nursery and childcare in Basel City: fees and subsidies
item.description: Guide to Child Custody in the Canton of Basel-City: Progressive Fees, Cantonal Subsidies, and Federal Family Tax Deductions. How to access services.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Childcare is a significant expense in the Swiss family budget - Progressive rates based on family income in each canton - Cantonal subsidies available for families with medium to low incomes - Federal and cantonal tax deductions for authorized childcare expenses
## Key facts - **What**: Childcare (daycare centers, childminders, after-school services) - Where: Canton of Basel-Stadt, Switzerland - Who: Families with children, cantonal administration - Scope: Progressive rates, subsidies, tax deductions - Basis: Calculation of rates based on net family income
### In the canton of Basel-Stadt: the childcare system In the canton of Basel-Stadt, as in the rest of Switzerland, childcare represents a significant expense in the household budget. Families have access to various options: [public or private daycare centers](nav:nursery), authorized childminders, and after-school services for school-aged children. The choice of childcare type depends on family needs, work schedules, and available budget.
The Swiss system provides progressive rates, calculated based on the family's net income from the previous year. This means that families with lower incomes pay reduced rates, while those with higher incomes bear greater amounts. The progressive mechanism ensures fairness in the system: those with less economic capacity benefit from affordable prices, while those who earn more contribute more.
The canton of Basel-Stadt provides subsidies to reduce the economic burden on families. However, the specific details of amounts, income thresholds, and administrative criteria for accessing subsidies are not yet available in the present source.
### Cantonal administration and access to services Each Swiss canton manages its own childcare support policy autonomously. In Basel-Stadt, cantonal subsidies are intended for families with specific income criteria. To access subsidies, families must submit an application to the competent cantonal office, providing documentation related to income and family situation.
The cantonal administration authorizes and monitors daycare centers, childminders, and after-school services. Parents can consult the official lists of authorized providers at the competent cantonal office or on the websites of the municipalities. Registration on the official list ensures that the facility meets the cantonal standards for quality, safety, and qualified personnel. ### Tax deductions and progressive mechanism
In Switzerland, childcare expenses benefit from favorable tax treatment, reducing the overall burden on the family budget. At the federal level (Direct Federal Tax), amounts paid to authorized childcare facilities can be deducted from taxable income up to an annual maximum (which varies depending on the family composition and is indexed each year). This deduction applies to the federal tax return submitted to the Federal Customs and Tax Administration.
The canton of Basel-Stadt, like all Swiss cantons, has the authority to provide additional deductions at the cantonal and municipal levels. This means that parents can obtain tax benefits both at the federal and cantonal levels, significantly reducing the net cost of childcare. The combination of progressive entry rates and tax deductions creates a progressive effect that protects lower-income families.
### Childcare options and family costs
The canton offers various childcare options, each with different characteristics and costs. Public daycare centers tend to offer more affordable rates (thanks to cantonal subsidies), while private ones range from premium facilities to conventional options. Family daycare is coordinated at the cantonal level and offers a more personalized and sometimes less costly alternative to daycare centers. After-school services are available for school-age children and assist during non-school periods.
The choice of [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in a Swiss family with children in childcare is significant. For many families, childcare represents a considerable percentage of the monthly budget before subsidies and deductions. This impact underscores the importance of knowing the available subsidies and optimizing tax deductions.
### Cantonal subsidies and access criteria
Each Swiss canton allocates funds to reduce childcare fees for families with limited incomes. In Basel-Stadt, subsidies are generally based on a combination of family income, number of children, and number of weekly childcare days. The exact calculation methods, income thresholds, and co-financing percentages remain in the process of being defined for specific local details.
Access to subsidies requires submitting an application to the competent cantonal office (usually the family office or social assistance office). Families must prove their income through official tax certificates and gross income statements. The administration reviews the application and communicates the amount of the contribution, which can cover a percentage of the monthly fee.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Procedure to access childcare and subsidies in Basel-Stadt
For families wishing to enroll a child in a childcare facility in the canton of Basel-Stadt, the typical procedure is as follows:
1. **Search for authorized facilities**: Visit the official website of the canton or the municipality of residence to consult the updated list of recognized daycare centers, family daycare services, and after-school services. All listed facilities have been authorized by the cantonal administration and meet legal requirements.
2. Contact and personalized quote: Contact the chosen facility directly to request information on availability, hours, and rates. Facilities calculate a personalized quote based on family income, commonly using the net income of the previous fiscal year and the number of children.
3. Subsidy application: If the family meets the income criteria, submit a formal application to the competent cantonal office (typically the social assistance or family office). Required documentation includes: copy of the tax return, income certificate, number of family members, number of weekly childcare days planned.
4. Evaluation and decision: The cantonal administration reviews the application within a set period (usually 2-4 weeks) and communicates in writing the amount of the subsidy granted, if the family is eligible. The contribution is often paid directly to the childcare facility.
### Tax planning and use of online tools
Before enrolling a child, parents should estimate the total annual cost based on their actual income and the chosen childcare facility. Using the [tax calculator](nav:calculator), it is possible to simulate the impact of childcare expenses on the overall tax burden and evaluate the available deductions at the federal and cantonal levels. This helps families better plan their annual budget.
For precise information on subsidies, current rates, access criteria, and administrative deadlines in the canton of Basel-Stadt, it is advisable to contact the competent cantonal office directly or consult the canton's official website. Specific data evolves annually based on cantonal budgets and local political decisions, so it is important to verify updated information before submitting the application.

item.title: Permit C Basel City: requirements and application
item.description: Residence permit C Basel: years required, integration, language skills and application procedure at the canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Permit C: long-term residence (10 years in general, 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens) - Requires integration: stable job, housing, language, local laws - Application at the cantonal migration office of Basel-Stadt - Renewable after 10 years, leads to ordinary naturalization
## Key facts
- What: Permit C (federal permanent residence permit) - Duration: 10 years for non-EU/EFTA foreigners; 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens - Issued by: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) in coordination with the canton - Where: Migration Office of the Canton of Basel-Stadt - Requirements: Socio-professional integration, local language, Swiss laws
The Permit C is the Swiss federal residence permit for foreigners intending to reside long-term. Managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) in coordination with the cantonal administrations, the Permit C is issued after at least 10 years of continuous legal residence (5 years for EU/EFTA citizens).
Unlike the Permit B (residence, renewable every 5 years) or the Permit L (short-term, up to 1 year), the Permit C offers prolonged residential stability and represents a concrete step towards ordinary Swiss naturalization.
### Integration and federal-cantonal criteria
To obtain the Permit C, federal and cantonal authorities assess the foreigner's integration into Swiss society. There is no rigid national standardized list, but the cantons — including Basel-Stadt — verify criteria such as:
- Stable professional situation (employment, self-employment, adequate income) - Permanent and stable housing in the canton - Knowledge of the local language (German, in the case of Basel) - Compliance with federal and cantonal Swiss legislation - Regular payment of AVS, IVA, cantonal and communal taxes
The process is individual: it is not automatic to reach 10 years of residence and receive the permit. Authorities also evaluate behavior, absence of significant criminal records, and overall socio-cultural integration.
### Permit C and next steps towards naturalization
Once obtained, the Permit C allows the foreigner to apply for ordinary Swiss naturalization after an additional 10 years of total residence (with possible double counting according to federal laws). Meanwhile, the Permit C is renewable at the end of its 10-year validity.
Who applies for the Permit C? Typically: workers who have been operating in Switzerland for years and reside stably, consolidated European immigrants in the labor market, professionals with long-term employment. Obtaining the Permit C has concrete fiscal and pension implications: the permanent resident is taxed in Switzerland on worldwide income (central element in the annual tax declaration), and fully contributes to AVS/AI/IVA/cantonal taxes as a stable resident. For more information on Swiss pension and the impact of status change, consult the guide on taxation for residents. Integration: what does it mean in practice?
Integration is not a uniform national quantitative metric, but rather it is evaluated by the canton and the municipality where you reside. According to federal regulations, integration requires four main dimensions:
Linguistic: Knowledge of the local language (German in Basel). Authorities usually verify this through direct interviews or certification. There is no official federal CEFR level required, but cantons generally require basic communication (A2 or B1 CEFR) for daily life: understanding work instructions, reading documents, interacting with schools or administration.
Socio-professional: Stable employment and sufficient income to support yourself without relying on public subsidies. Your employer may be contacted to verify your employment status.
Legal and civil: Absence of significant criminal records, regular payment of taxes and social contributions, and general compliance with Swiss laws (does not require detailed knowledge of the penal code, but correct conduct).
Cultural: Integration into the local community (use of public services, civic participation, social interactions). It is not mandatory to be a volunteer in associations, but it facilitates a positive evaluation.
Application procedures: the role of the canton and the SEM
The formal procedure is divided between the federal SEM and the Basel-Stadt cantonal migration office:
Phase 1 (Canton): You or your employer submit the application to the Basel-Stadt migration office. The required documents generally include: valid passport, residence certificate, current employment contract, recent pay slips, Swiss federal criminal record certificate, tax declaration for the last 2-3 years, proof of accommodation (rental or ownership contract), passport photo.
Phase 2 (Canton-SEM): The canton verifies integration based on the documentation and local checks, then sends the complete file to the SEM for federal evaluation.
Phase 3 (SEM): The SEM examines integration through consultations with the police and financial administration, then approves or denies, notifying the canton of the decision.
The overall duration is not fixed by federal regulation and is variable (from a few weeks to several months depending on administrative workload and completeness of the application). Basel-Stadt may publish average times on the migration office website.
Knowledge of local laws and pension system
The canton of Basel-Stadt may verify familiarity with cantonal laws (rights and duties, cohabitation regulations). This is typically not a formal exam but is evaluated during the integration interview. Key element: familiarity with Swiss public order, labor rights, cantonal school system if relevant (for example, if you have children).
Once you obtain the C permit, taxation changes significantly: you are a permanent Swiss resident and the canton exercises fiscal authority over worldwide income (not just Swiss earnings). AVS/AI contributions continue at the standard dependent rate (5.3% of salary, employer adds 5.3%), but your pension accreditation improves, bringing you closer to the 43 years of contributions paid (men) or 42 years (women) for full AVS pension. To understand the impact on [supplementary pension LPP and AVS](nav:pension), consult federal resources on pensions.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to apply: step-by-step procedure
Step 1: Check prerequisites
Before applying, verify: Do you have at least 10 years of continuous legal residence in Switzerland with a valid L or B permit? Are you an EU/EFTA citizen (in which case, count 5 years)? Do you currently and legally reside in the canton of Basel-Stadt? If the answer is yes to all questions, proceed to the next steps.
Step 2: Gather official documents
Contact the migration office of the canton of Basel-Stadt directly to obtain the complete and up-to-date list. Generally, the essential documents include:
- Valid passport or identity card - Official certificate of residence (not older than 3 months) - Current employment contract or self-employment declaration - Last 2-3 pay slips (or self-employed balance sheet for the last 2 years) - Swiss federal criminal record certificate (requestable online via the federal portal) - Federal and cantonal tax declarations for the last 2-3 years - Rental contract or property certificate (proof of stable housing) - Official passport photo (if required)
Step 3: Submit application and attend interview
Request an appointment at the Basel-Stadt migration office. Some cantons require online booking, others manage it at the counter. During the interview: bring all original documents in certified copy, the interview is conducted in German (basic level, no linguistic perfection required), prepare answers on employment, language integration, respect for laws, future projects in Switzerland.
Step 4: Federal checks and administrative decision
The cantonal office transmits the complete file to the SEM. The State Secretariat for Migration verifies integration through consultations with cantonal police authorities and financial administration. The duration of this phase varies: from a few weeks to several months depending on the workload and clarity of the documents.
Step 5: Reception of permit C and final formalities
Once the application is approved, you will receive the permit C from the canton (physical document or digital access according to cantonal procedures). Validity: 10 years from the date of issue, renewable at the end through a new renewal application.
### Deadlines, contacts, and planning
There is no universal federal deadline for submitting an application. However, if you are close to 10 years (or 5 if EU/EFTA) of residence, it is advisable to start the process 6-12 months before the threshold date to avoid gaps and manage administrative times. The application has no fixed federal costs, but some cantons may require a cantonal administrative fee (check with the local office).
For specific details of Basel-Stadt:
- Basel-Stadt migration office: Consult the official website of the canton of Basel-Stadt in the administration and residence rights section - SEM (State Secretariat for Migration): National portal with guides, forms, and information on federal permits
### Next steps after permit C
Once you have obtained permit C, you can start planning for ordinary Swiss naturalization (requires 10 years of residence AFTER the issuance of permit C, with possible double counting depending on age and acquisition channel). In parallel, permit C improves your tax and pension position: you are subject to worldwide taxation, accrue full AVS contributions, and consolidate pension rights.
To plan the tax impact of permit C on your income and contributions: calculate your federal, cantonal, and municipal taxes with our tax and contribution calculator. Knowing the estimated tax burden as a permanent resident helps you plan your budget and evaluate the convenience of the transfer.

item.title: AVS and complementary services in the Canton of Graubünden
item.description: First pillar, contribution gaps and access to supplementary benefits: a practical guide for residents and taxpayers of the Canton of Graubünden.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - AVS is the first Swiss pillar: basic insurance with pension calculated on contribution years - Supplementary benefits intervene if AVS does not cover the minimum living standard - Cantonal compensation fund in Graubünden manages requests and payments
## Key facts - **What**: AVS (1st pillar) + supplementary benefits for Graubünden residents - Where: Graubünden Cantonal Compensation Fund - When: Application at the reference age (65 years for the majority) - Who: Federal Social Insurance Office (national standards) + cantonal administration (supplementary benefits) - Requirement: At least one year of contributions paid for the right to the minimum AVS benefit
### The role of AVS in the Canton of Graubünden The AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance) is the first pillar of Swiss social security. In the Canton of Graubünden, as in every canton, the cantonal compensation fund manages pension requests and related benefits. The FSO (Federal Social Insurance Office) sets the national criteria and thresholds, while the cantonal administration manages the supplementary benefits and checks the access requirements.
The AVS pension is calculated considering the years of contributions paid as an employee, self-employed, or unemployed. One year of minimum contribution is sufficient to access a minimum benefit, while a full career (43 years for men, 42 for women until 2025) allows reaching the maximum national pension. The average career income is another element: the higher the average income paid, the higher the pension.
### Supplementary benefits: the bridge to the minimum living standard When the AVS pension does not cover the basic expenses to live with dignity, supplementary benefits to AVS intervene. These are not welfare aids but rights derived from a national insurance system with precise access thresholds. In the Canton of Graubünden, the compensation fund assesses the assets, income from other pillars (LPP), and family situation to determine if the AVS pension is insufficient.
The minimum living standard is established by federal law and varies slightly by canton. Supplementary benefits fill the gap between the AVS pension actually paid and the amount that guarantees economic dignity.
### Contribution gaps: causes and consequences Periods of unemployment, illness, irregular or underreported work generate contribution gaps. Those who have interrupted their career for caregiving (assisting family members) may also present years without contributions. The cantonal compensation fund examines the gaps and evaluates if there are legitimate reasons (involuntary unemployment, certified work incapacity, etc.). In the absence of legitimate reasons, the pension decreases proportionally: a career with a 2-year gap out of 43 will have a pension reduction calculated on a proportional basis.
Furthermore, if the gap is so large that it excludes the right to the minimum benefit (less than 1 year of contributions), there will be no AVS pension, but the person may still access supplementary benefits if in a situation of need. ### Calculation of the pension: from contributions to monthly pension
The monthly AVS pension is determined by the average income earned during the career. This average income is not simply calculated as an arithmetic mean: the Swiss system applies a formula that takes into account the evolution of salaries over time. Recent periods have a greater weight than distant ones. The calculated average income is then multiplied by the pension rate, which varies depending on the retirement age and gender.
A contributor who has paid contributions throughout their career will receive a higher pension than someone with gaps. For example, a hypothetical scenario: a person with 40 years of regular contributions will have a stronger base compared to someone with 35 years (a 5-year difference affects the final pension). The cantonal compensation fund performs this calculation before communicating the expected pension amount.
Furthermore, those who have funds in the second pillar (LPP/BVG) see their AVS benefit coordinated with the LPP value. This means that a certain amount of the LPP benefit (the coordination deduction) is subtracted from the AVS pension calculation to avoid double payments. This mechanism is technical but important: it does not increase the total pension but distributes it between AVS and LPP.
### Thresholds for access to supplementary benefits
After calculating the AVS pension, the cantonal fund evaluates whether this covers the minimum living expenses. Supplementary benefits are granted if the income from all sources (AVS, LPP, rents, family donations, etc.) is below the minimum living standard set by federal law.
The minimum living standard includes: - Food and housing for the person - Medical expenses not covered by health insurance (prescriptions not supported by LAMal/KVG) - Health insurance itself (LAMal/KVG premiums) - Public transportation expenses for essential needs
Each canton slightly adapts these criteria, but the federal guidelines remain the same. In the Canton of Grisons, the compensation fund verifies the assets: if the person owns real estate, savings, or other assets, these are considered. A threshold of exempt assets (personal belongings, main residence) is protected, but values above this limit reduce access to benefits.
### Supplementary benefits vs. social assistance
It is crucial not to confuse supplementary AVS benefits with municipal social assistance. The former are managed at the federal/cantonal level and are a right derived from the payment of contributions (even if minimal). Social assistance is a municipal safety net for those without income and not entitled to other benefits. Supplementary benefits have insurance dignity; assistance is precautionary support.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to submit a request in the Canton of Grisons
The AVS application must be submitted to the compensation fund of the Canton of Grisons within 3 months from the date of eligibility (usually the month following the 65th birthday). The application can be submitted to the cantonal compensation fund office via the official form, available online or at the counter. The form requires complete personal data, AVS insurance number, declaration of current residence in Grisons, and authorization for data verification with other federal and cantonal offices.
### Essential Documentation
The compensation fund requires: - Birth certificate (for identity verification) - Marriage certificate and any divorce certificates (to verify changes in marital status) - Income tax returns for the past 2-3 years (to assess wealth and income from other sources) - LPP status certification (if the applicant has joined pension funds) - Declaration of real estate assets (ownership, mortgages, rental income received) - Recent bank statements (to assess liquid assets)
If the applicant has lived or worked in other cantons, they must provide certificates from previous compensation funds to ensure that all contribution years have been correctly registered in the federal system.
### Deadlines and Procedure
After submitting the application, the Grisons compensation fund has 30-45 days to perform preliminary checks. If the application is complete, the first payment may occur within 2-3 months of the request. Administrative holidays (August, end of year) can extend the processing time.
Once approved, the AVS pension is paid monthly into the specified bank account. If the applicant is also entitled to supplementary benefits, the fund will communicate this in a separate notice, specifying the additional monthly amount and conditions (e.g., annual wealth checks).
Use this tool to estimate the expected pension amount before submitting the official request. In case of significant contribution gaps, the [calculator](nav:calculator) can help simulate scenarios of reduced pensions. Contact the compensation fund of the Canton of Grisons directly for free preliminary advice: the fund is legally obligated to provide information about your rights. To evaluate the minimum budget in the Canton of Grisons and plan your pension, consult [our cost of living tool](nav:cost-of-living).

item.title: Naturalization in Graubünden: requirements and procedure
item.description: How to become a Swiss citizen in the canton of Graubünden. Federal route, cantonal requirements, language and integration tests, taxes and duration of the procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Ordinary naturalization requires 10 years of residence with a C permit in Switzerland - The canton of Graubünden applies specific language and integration tests - Naturalization taxes are due, calculated by the municipality of residence - The procedure duration varies according to the Graubünden municipality
## Key facts - **What**: Federal ordinary naturalization + Graubünden cantonal requirements - When: After 10 years of residence with a C permit (5 years for EU/EFTA citizens) - Where: Canton of Graubünden - Who: Applicant + Graubünden cantonal and municipal authorities - Permit: C permit (domicile) mandatory throughout the procedure
Ordinary naturalization in Switzerland follows a strictly defined federal path, but each canton — including Graubünden — adds its own requirements that vary from municipality to municipality. Those wishing to become Swiss citizens in the canton of Graubünden must first meet the federal criteria: at least 10 years of uninterrupted residence with a C permit (domicile permit). This term can be reduced to five years for citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association. In addition to the standard count, Swiss law also allows double counting of the residence period between the ages of 8 and 18: one year of residence in that interval counts as two years for naturalization purposes, potentially reducing the overall term.
### The federal framework of naturalization
In addition to the ten years of residence (or EU/EFTA regional variants), federal law requires uninterrupted possession of a C permit. This means that the applicant must not have suspended their right of residence, must not have committed serious criminal offenses, and must demonstrate a positive attitude towards Switzerland and its institutions. During the naturalization process, the candidate remains subject to federal and cantonal tax regulations: it is important to stay up-to-date on one's tax situation and regularly file the [tax return](nav:tax-return) according to the deadlines and forms prescribed by the competent authorities.
The federal procedure represents the first level of evaluation: it is a national screening that verifies basic eligibility. The C permit is not automatic after ten years; it is a residence title renewable every ten years, which can be revoked if the applicant commits crimes or is considered a threat to public order. Naturalization transforms the C permit into permanent citizenship: no expiration, no renewal, federal, cantonal, and municipal political rights.
In Graubünden, as in all Swiss cantons, the federal path is combined with specific cantonal and municipal requirements. The canton of Graubünden and its municipalities require language tests, integration tests, payment of naturalization taxes, and an evaluation of the candidate's civil conduct. These additional elements reflect the Swiss federalist principle: naturalization is primarily a cantonal-municipal decision, while operating within the basic federal framework. ### Specific requirements of the canton of Graubünden The canton of Graubünden exercises decision-making authority over the naturalization of candidates, subject to compliance with federal criteria. This means that even after acquiring ten years of residence with a C permit, the candidate must still obtain the approval of the Graubünden authorities. The municipalities of Graubünden — particularly Chur, Davos, Poschiavo, and dozens of other centers — are responsible for the processing of the application, the collection of documents, the verification of conduct, and the final decision. Each municipality may have slightly different procedures, although all operate within the cantonal framework. It is therefore crucial to contact the naturalization office of your municipality as soon as possible, from the first year of residence with a C permit, to learn about the exact requirements and waiting times. The canton of Graubünden and its municipalities impose language tests in Italian, Romansh, or German (depending on the Graubünden region) and integration tests into Swiss society. These tests assess the candidate's level of knowledge of the local language and familiarity with institutions, constitutional values, history, and Swiss culture. Passing these tests is mandatory. Additionally, the canton requires the payment of naturalization taxes. The amount varies from municipality to municipality and is determined by the municipal law of Graubünden, not by a national federal tariff. Some municipalities apply a fixed fee, while others base the cost on a multiple of the candidate's income or assets. This cantonal differentiation reflects Swiss communal sovereignty in matters of naturalization: there is no uniform national price. ### Municipal variability and access to rights post-naturalization An often overlooked aspect is the verification of civil conduct. The canton of Graubünden and individual municipalities check criminal records, psychiatric medical records (if relevant), bankruptcy proceedings, and the candidate's behavior in the local community. Testimonies from neighbors, employers, or municipal representatives can influence the decision. Even minor violations (unpaid traffic fines, civil disputes, harassment complaints) can delay or block approval. This evaluation is subjective and depends on local authorities, which is why it is essential to maintain an impeccable reputation throughout the period of residence in Switzerland. Acquiring Swiss citizenship grants the new citizen access to the [mandatory pension systems AVS and LPP](nav:pension), which are fundamental for social protection in case of old age, disability, or death. Automatic registration in the pension system is done through the employer (for the professional LPP regime) and the federal administration (for the basic AVS pension). These systems represent a central pillar of Swiss social security and will significantly influence future salary deductions and contributions made.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to proceed: the naturalization process in Graubünden
Ordinary naturalization in Graubünden follows a process with specific steps. The candidate must first verify that they possess a C permit and have completed ten years of uninterrupted residence (or five years if they are a citizen of the EU/EFTA). Once these federal criteria are met, the next step is to contact the naturalization office of the municipality where they reside. There is no centralized cantonal office for naturalization: each municipality in Graubünden manages the applications of its residents independently.
The first step is to obtain the official naturalization application form. The form must be completed and signed by the candidate. Simultaneously, the applicant must gather supporting documents: residence certificate, original C permit, federal criminal record extract, certificate of good conduct from the municipality of residence, identity documents (passport or ID card of the country of origin), and income or real estate ownership certificates (the latter may be required if the municipality bases taxes on assets). Some municipalities also require a declaration of loyalty to Swiss constitutional values, although this is not mandatory at the federal level.
Once the application is submitted and the preliminary fee is paid (if required by the municipality), the investigation begins. The municipality verifies the data, contacts the federal authorities to confirm the C permit, obtains the criminal record, and summons the candidate for the language test. The language test in Graubünden varies by region: in the Italian-speaking areas (Poschiavo, Bregaglia) the test is in Italian, in the Romansh-speaking areas (Upper Engadine, Surselva) it is in Romansh, and in the German-speaking areas it is in German. The candidate must reach a B1 level according to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR). The integration test covers questions on Swiss history, rights and duties of citizenship, state secularism, and principles of direct democracy.
### Timelines and conclusion of the procedure
The overall duration of the procedure varies: from six months to two years, depending on the workload of the municipal office and the speed at which the candidate provides documents. Once the tests are passed and the checks are completed, the municipality presents the application to the canton for final cantonal approval. Finally, the Parliament of the Canton of Graubünden votes on the naturalization decree (a traditional procedure in many cantons). Once this step is completed, the candidate receives the naturalization certificate and acquires Swiss citizenship.
To calculate and understand the tax implications of naturalization — including new inheritance rights, changes in local and federal taxation, and modifications to VAT calculation — consult the [Swiss tax calculator](nav:calculator). This tool will help you plan your tax situation after acquiring Swiss citizenship.

item.title: Rentals in Grisons: fees, deposit and rental rights
item.description: Practical guide to Swiss tenancy law: how security deposit, rent dispute and cancellation terms work in the Canton of Graubünden.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The security deposit cannot exceed 3 months of rent and is in the name of the tenant - The dispute of the initial fee must be made within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Termination requires terms of 1, 2 or 3 months depending on the year of validity of the contract
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss lease right, governed by articles 253+ of the Code of Obligations - Where: Canton of Graubünden and uniformly throughout Switzerland - Maximum deposit: 3 months monthly rent - Deposit account: Restricted and exclusively in the name of the tenant - Dispute: Within 30 days to the cantonal conciliation authority - First year cancellation: 1 month; from the second to the ninth year: 2 months; from the tenth: 3 months
The right to rent in Switzerland is federal and applies identically in every canton, including Graubünden. The relationship between landlord and tenant is governed by articles 253 et seq. of the Code of Obligations, which establish clear and unavoidable mutual rights and duties.
Those who reside in the Canton of Graubünden and rent a home enjoy the same protections guaranteed at the national level. There are no exceptions or cantonal variations to the fundamental principles: the landlord cannot request more than what is established by law, the tenant has the right to challenge unjust fees, and the termination of the relationship must follow precise terms and procedures.
### Security Deposit: Tenant Protection
The ### Challenging the initial rent: the tenant's right
If the rent proposed by the landlord appears unjust or significantly higher than the rents for similar accommodations in the area, the tenant has the right to challenge it. The challenge must be made within 30 days of signing the contract and must be submitted to the rental conciliation authority of the Canton of Grisons.
The authority examines the request and verifies whether the rent is indeed unjust based on objective elements: size, location, state of preservation, available services, comparable rents in the geographical area. You can consult the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in your region to compare standard rents. If the authority finds the appeal justified, it can order a rent reduction.
This procedure is free for the tenant or involves minimal costs and does not require the intervention of a lawyer. It represents a concrete and accessible tool to protect tenants from abusive demands.
### Termination of the contract: legal terms and procedures
The termination must be communicated using the official form provided by the Canton of Grisons. Informal communications (email, telephone, verbal communication) are not legally valid, regardless of how they were agreed upon.
The notice periods depend on the year of the contract's validity: one month during the first year, two months from the second to the ninth year, and three months from the tenth year onwards. The termination deadline must coincide with December 31 or the last day of a month.
The landlord cannot terminate a contract within the first three years if the reason is an increase in rent. The tenant has similar protections. The termination must respect legitimate reasons: personal need of the landlord (relocation, own residence) or other reasons contemplated by the law. A termination presented during a rent challenge procedure before the conciliation authority is considered illegitimate and can be contested.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-step procedure: how to legally terminate a lease
To end a lease contract in the Canton of Graubünden according to the rules, follow these concrete steps:
**1. Obtain the form**: Request the official termination form from the competent office of the Canton of Graubünden for rental matters. The form is also available on the official website of the canton.
2. Fill it out carefully: Enter the required data: tenant and landlord's name, complete address of the property, start date of the contract, reason for termination (if provided by the contract), end date of the lease.
3. Respect the notice period: Calculate the notice period based on the year of validity (1, 2, or 3 months from the date you send the form). The end date must fall on December 31 or the last day of a month.
4. Send the completed form: Deliver the form by registered mail or in person with a receipt to the landlord (or to the tenant, if you are the landlord). Keep a signed copy as proof.
5. Prepare the return of the property: By the agreed date, completely vacate the apartment. Document the final state of the premises and agree with the landlord on the date of key return and deposit refund.
### When to resort to the conciliation authority
If the landlord refuses to return the security deposit, unjustifiably contests the termination, or withholds the deposit without reason, you can resort to the conciliation authority for rental matters. This instance resolves disputes without the need to resort to the cantonal court and is available free of charge or at minimal cost.
The conciliation authority is present in every canton and provides free consultations on procedures. Contact it through the official website of the Canton of Graubünden.

item.title: Buying a house in Graubünden: a guide to funds and mortgages
item.description: Procedure, own funds, mortgage loan and taxation on three levels. How to buy a property in Switzerland complying with federal and cantonal regulations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Buying a house in Switzerland is regulated by well-defined federal and cantonal laws - Taxation is structured at three levels: federal, cantonal, and municipal - Own funds and mortgage sustainability are assessed according to uniform banking criteria - Notary fees and transfer tax vary by canton
## Key facts - **What**: Purchase of real estate through a notarial procedure - Where: Canton of Graubünden and other Swiss cantons - Who: Resident buyer or with appropriate permit - When: Procedure from 2 to 4 months from offer to property transfer - Basis: Federal civil law (Code of Obligations) + specific cantonal laws
Buying a house in the Canton of Graubünden involves a procedure regulated by well-defined federal and cantonal laws. The decision to become owners involves a careful evaluation of three crucial elements: the availability of own funds, the sustainability of the mortgage, and the impact of taxation at three levels (federal, cantonal, and municipal). There is no special regime for Graubünden, but the canton applies its own transfer tax rates and notarial rules, exactly as happens in every other Swiss canton.
### Own funds and credit assessment
To obtain a mortgage from a Swiss bank, the prospective owner must have a share of own funds. The sustainability criterion is universal: the amount of the monthly amortization installment must not exceed a certain percentage of the available gross income. Graubünden and all Swiss residents are subject to the same creditworthiness assessment according to prudential guidelines defined at the federal level by the Swiss National Bank (SNB).
The mortgage application includes a check of the financial solidity of the borrower: income stability, credit history, other liabilities. Banks in Switzerland check the financing capacity in the same way regardless of the geographical region. The bank requires an estimate of the property value and an analysis of the ratio between the property value and the requested mortgage amount (loan-to-value ratio). Once the application is approved, the bank issues a mortgage pre-approval valid for a limited period, within which the buyer must proceed with the final notarial deed. ### Three-tier taxation: how it works in Switzerland
The taxation of a property is organized on three distinct levels. The federal direct tax (IFD) is calculated by the Federal Department of Finance by applying a uniform federal rate to the net taxable income of the property. Each canton has its own tax law and different rates: in the canton of Graubünden, as in the other 25 cantons, a cantonal multiplier is applied to the federal tax base. Finally, the municipalities apply their own multiplier to the cantonal base, creating further variability. Two municipalities in the same canton can have significantly different tax burdens.
For those who purchase a house as their primary residence, ordinary taxation includes the imputed net income (if not rented) or the actual rental income. However, mortgage interest is deductible from taxable income at the federal and cantonal levels, reducing the tax due. This deduction represents a significant tax advantage in the early years of the mortgage, when the interest portion is higher compared to the principal repayment.
### Transfer tax and notarial procedure
When purchasing a house, the notarial procedure is mandatory in Switzerland. The notary's office drafts the property transfer deeds and takes care of the registration with the land registry. Notarial fees (professional fees and administrative expenses) are regulated on a cantonal basis. In the canton of Graubünden, as in other cantons, the notary's fee is generally proportional to the value of the property and is not fixed at the federal level. The exact amount varies depending on the complexity of the deed and the rates applied by the notary's office.
The transfer tax (also called registration tax or real estate transfer tax) is a cantonal and municipal tax that applies to the transfer of property ownership. Each canton has its own rate, often on a progressive basis. The canton of Graubünden, like all Swiss cantons, has defined its own regulations regarding transfer tax. This tax is due by the buyer and is paid to the cantonal administration within the deadlines set by cantonal law. In the notarial procedure, it is the notary's office that takes care of the calculation and communication to the cantonal tax authority.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-step procedure for purchasing a property
The procedure for purchasing a house in Switzerland follows well-defined steps. First, verify your financing capacity by contacting the bank: find out the maximum mortgage amount suitable and the percentage of own funds required (usually between 10% and 20% of the purchase price). Then, start your property search in the Canton of Graubünden through national real estate portals or by contacting local specialized real estate agents.
Once you have identified the property, the real estate agent or seller proposes a preliminary purchase agreement (letter of intent). This phase is NOT legally binding but sets the essential details of the offer: price, amounts related to the property (boiler, installations), delivery date. Then, submit the offer to your bank to start the mortgage application process. The bank performs an appraisal (valuation) of the property and a credit check of the borrower. This process usually takes 2-4 weeks.
Once the mortgage is approved, the notary office drafts the sales contract in authentic form (mandatory in Switzerland). The notarial contract includes all conditions of the sale and is registered with the municipal cadastre. During the signing of the notarial deed, the own funds are paid, and the mortgage documents are signed with the bank. The notary office then coordinates the transfer of funds from the bank to the seller and the registration of the property in the name of the buyer. This phase concludes the legal transfer of ownership.
Finally, report the purchase to the cantonal tax administration (Tax Office of the Canton of Graubünden) within the prescribed deadlines. The transfer tax will be communicated in a separate notice. The municipal administration will also register your name in the land register and communicate the new cadastral data to the local authorities for updating the tax rolls.
### Resources for further information
For an accurate assessment of the mortgage sustainability, use a dedicated calculation tool that simulates the monthly installment amount based on realistic assumptions of interest rate and amortization period. The [tax return](nav:tax-return) is the document where to indicate the deductions related to the purchase and the mortgage. Contact a real estate agent specialized in the Canton of Graubünden, request a mortgage pre-approval from your bank, and start your property search with realistic expectations of price and location.
